ten: First Day of Each Lunar Month
moTa: On the first day of every lunar month, many Vietnamese families light incense, eat vegetarian meals or visit a temple to begin the month with a calm mind. It is a moment to look back on the past month, set one small intention and remember to slow down.
trangTri: Yellow chrysanthemums on the altar
A plate of five-colored fruit
A small oil lamp beside the incense burner
Fresh bodhi leaves on the courtyard tree
nhiemVu: Light a virtual incense stick in the main hall
Write one small intention for the new month
Sit quietly for 3 minutes with the temple bell
Visit the Wishing Tree and send kind wishes to others

ten: Full Moon of Each Lunar Month
moTa: The full-moon day in the middle of each lunar month. In Buddhist tradition, monastics recite the precepts on the full moon and new moon; lay people often eat vegetarian, visit temples and listen to teachings. The round moon evokes a clear, complete and peaceful mind.
trangTri: A full moon above the temple roof
Paper lanterns along the entrance path
White lotuses in the pond
Light incense smoke drifting across the courtyard
nhiemVu: Watch the full moon from the courtyard for one silent minute
Light virtual lamps along the path
Read a short teaching on loving-kindness
Note three things you are grateful for this month

moTa: The first day of the lunar new year; the event continues through the second and third days of Tết. Families reunite, exchange New Year wishes and make their first temple visit of the year. The first day of Tết is also the celebration day of Maitreya Buddha, the future Buddha whose joyful smile stands for happiness and generosity of heart.
trangTri: Yellow apricot and pink peach blossom branches
Red parallel couplets beside the three-entrance gate
Red lanterns along the corridors
A five-fruit tray
A smiling Maitreya statue in the front hall
nhiemVu: Make your first temple visit: light virtual incense in the main hall
Send a New Year wish to a loved one
Draw a New Year fortune stick for reflection
Write one thing to let go of and one thing to nurture this year
Smile with Maitreya and give someone a sincere compliment

ten: First Full Moon – Thượng Nguyên Festival
moTa: The first full moon of the year, also called the Thượng Nguyên or Lantern Festival. A Vietnamese saying holds that a year of temple visits does not equal the first full moon, so temples are often busy with people praying for their families' peace. The day is also linked with poetry and moonlit lantern festivities.
trangTri: Floating lotus lanterns on the pond
The first full moon of spring
Colorful lanterns along the path
A tea table with paper for poems
nhiemVu: Release a virtual floating lantern with a wish for peace
Write or copy a line of poetry about the spring moon
Light incense for your family's well-being
Read others' wishes and send them kind thoughts

moTa: Commemorates the day Prince Siddhartha left the palace to seek a path to freedom from suffering for all beings. It is a time to reflect on letting go of unnecessary attachments and on the resolve to pursue what is good.
trangTri: A painting of the Prince leaving the palace on a white horse
Golden lotuses on both sides of the main hall
White lanterns
Five-colored Buddhist flags
nhiemVu: Choose one small habit to let go of this week
Tidy up a corner of your home or your phone
Sit quietly for 5 minutes following your breath
Read a short summary of the Prince's renunciation story

moTa: Remembers the Buddha's passing into final Nirvana at Kushinagar after more than forty years of teaching. His last reminder is often recalled as an encouragement to strive diligently on one's own. A day for quiet remembrance and reflection on impermanence.
trangTri: A reclining Buddha resting beneath sala trees
White lotuses
Small candles around the statue
Leaves softly falling on the courtyard
nhiemVu: Light a virtual memorial candle
Sit in silence for 3 minutes reflecting on impermanence
Write one thing you want to cherish more today
Water the bodhi tree in the courtyard

moTa: Celebrates the birth of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, known in Vietnam as Quan Thế Âm. The Bodhisattva embodies great compassion, listening to the cries of all beings. Many people visit temples, eat vegetarian food and practice listening to others with empathy.
trangTri: A Quan Âm statue holding a vase with a willow branch
Pink lotuses in the pond
White lanterns along the corridor
A vase of white tuberoses
nhiemVu: Listen fully to a loved one without interrupting
Send a caring message to someone going through a hard time
Light virtual incense before the Quan Âm shrine
Write a wish for someone else, not for yourself

moTa: In Vietnam, the Cold Food Festival is associated with bánh trôi and bánh chay, small round glutinous rice dumplings. Many families make them and offer them to their ancestors in gratitude. Shaping the little white dumplings together is also a time to gather and share old stories.
trangTri: A plate of rice dumplings on the altar
A small bowl of sweet soup on a wooden tray
White pomelo blossoms
A bamboo tray of drying rice flour
nhiemVu: Shape virtual rice dumplings with the young novices
Offer a plate of dumplings on the ancestral altar
Ask a grandparent or parent about a memory from long ago
Share the childhood dish you miss the most

moTa: The day of Manjushri Bodhisattva, who represents wisdom and is often shown riding a blue lion, holding the sword of wisdom that cuts through ignorance. A day that encourages learning, clear thinking and honestly reviewing what we understand.
trangTri: A statue of Manjushri riding a lion
Wooden bookshelves in the temple library
A warm study lamp
Calligraphy brushes and an ink stone
nhiemVu: Read one page of a book you have been saving
Learn something new and write it down in one sentence
Light a virtual lamp of wisdom in the library
Send encouragement to someone studying for exams

moTa: Celebrates the birth of Shakyamuni Buddha in Lumbini Garden. In Vietnam, Vesak is held on the full moon of the fourth lunar month with the bathing-the-Buddha ceremony, lantern processions, flags and flowers. It is a major festival honoring the birth of the Awakened One and reminding everyone to nurture the seed of mindfulness.
trangTri: Five-colored Buddhist flags across the courtyard
A bathing altar with the infant Buddha statue
Multicolored lotus lanterns
A flower arch at the three-entrance gate
A lotus pond in full bloom
nhiemVu: Join the virtual bathing-the-Buddha ceremony
Hang a lotus lantern along the path
Do a small kind deed for someone near you
Send Vesak greetings to your friends
Sit quietly for 5 minutes listening to the temple bell

moTa: The Đoan Ngọ Festival, popularly called the day of "killing inner bugs", falls in the middle of summer. Families eat fresh fruit, fermented sticky rice and lye rice cakes, and pay attention to their health as the weather turns hot. It is also a time to gather and look after one another.
trangTri: Baskets of plums, lychees and watermelon
A small bowl of fermented sticky rice
A bundle of mugwort hung by the door
Lye rice cakes wrapped in leaves
nhiemVu: Drink a glass of water and stretch for 1 minute
Arrange a virtual tray of summer fruit
Message a relative to ask how they are
Pick herbal leaves in the temple garden

moTa: Commemorates the enlightenment of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, one of the three Quan Âm days of the year. A reminder to cultivate compassion through concrete actions, helping others without expecting anything in return.
trangTri: A standing Quan Âm statue on a lotus throne
A summer pond of pink lotuses
Blue glass lamps
White jasmine flowers
nhiemVu: Do one helpful thing without telling anyone
Light virtual incense before the Quan Âm shrine
Float a virtual lotus leaf on the pond with a wish for peace
Write a wish for all living beings

moTa: The Vu Lan festival of filial gratitude, rooted in the story of Venerable Maudgalyayana and his love for his mother. It is a season to remember parents and grandparents; many wear a rose on their shirt: red if their parents are living, white if they have passed away. Folk tradition also calls this day the pardon day for wandering souls.
trangTri: Red and white roses
Floating lanterns on the pond
An ancestral altar with incense and flowers
A banner reading "Vu Lan – Gratitude to Parents"
nhiemVu: Pin a virtual rose to your shirt
Call or message your parents to say thank you
Release a floating lantern in memory of loved ones who have passed
Write a fond memory of your grandparents or parents
Have a simple vegetarian meal

moTa: The day of Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva, associated with the great vow to help beings in realms of suffering and with filial devotion. A time to dedicate merit to those who have passed away. Note: if the seventh lunar month has only 29 days that year, the event takes place on the 29th.
trangTri: A Ksitigarbha statue holding a ringed staff and a jewel
Soft golden candlelight
White chrysanthemums
A wooden prayer bead string
nhiemVu: Light a virtual candle dedicated to those who have passed
Write a gentle message of remembrance
Chant or sit in silence for 3 minutes
Pick up one piece of real litter near where you live

moTa: The Mid-Autumn Festival, also known as the Reunion Festival or Children's Festival, when the moon is at its brightest and roundest. Children parade with star lanterns and share a moon feast; adults admire the moon over tea and mooncakes. A time for families to gather together.
trangTri: Star lanterns and carp lanterns
A moon feast tray with baked and sticky mooncakes
A large full moon above the bell tower
A lion dance head
Pomelos and red persimmons
nhiemVu: Parade a virtual star lantern around the courtyard
Set up a Mid-Autumn feast with the young novices
Watch the moon and write a wish for your family
Tell a Mid-Autumn story to a child

moTa: Commemorates the renunciation of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, the last Quan Âm day of the year. A time to reflect on setting aside selfishness to live for others, and on keeping a gentle heart amid daily busyness.
trangTri: A Quan Âm statue meditating on a rocky mountain
An autumn bamboo grove
Pale yellow lanterns
Autumn chrysanthemums
nhiemVu: Let someone else go first in one small thing today
Light virtual incense before the Quan Âm shrine
Walk slowly through the temple bamboo grove
Write a thank-you note to someone who once helped you

moTa: The day of the Medicine Buddha, Lord of Lapis Lazuli Light, associated with twelve great vows for the health of body and mind. A time to care for your own health and that of your loved ones, rest when needed and live in moderation. If the ninth lunar month has only 29 days, the event takes place on the 29th.
trangTri: A Medicine Buddha statue holding a medicine jar
Deep blue lapis lamps
A garden of traditional medicinal herbs
A pot of herbal tea
nhiemVu: Walk for 10 minutes or stretch gently
Go to bed earlier than usual tonight
Message someone who is unwell
Water the herb garden in the temple

ten: Hạ Nguyên Festival – Tenth-Month Full Moon
moTa: The full moon of the tenth lunar month, also called the Hạ Nguyên or New Rice Festival, linked with the year's final harvest in many rural areas. People offer green rice flakes, sticky rice and newly harvested rice to their ancestors, giving thanks to heaven and earth and to those who grow the rice.
trangTri: Sheaves of golden ripe rice
Plates of green rice flakes and new sticky rice
The last full moon of autumn
Bamboo trays of drying paddy
nhiemVu: Offer a virtual plate of new-rice sticky rice on the altar
Write a thank-you to the farmers
Finish your meal today without wasting food
List three things you have harvested this year

moTa: The day of Amitabha Buddha, the Buddha of the Western Pure Land in the Pure Land tradition, deeply familiar to Vietnamese people through the recitation "Nam mô A Di Đà Phật". A time to practice reciting the Buddha's name, keep a peaceful mind and turn toward goodness.
trangTri: An Amitabha statue with a radiant halo
A seven-jeweled lotus pond
Warm golden light throughout the main hall
Prayer beads and a wooden fish drum
nhiemVu: Recite "Nam mô A Di Đà Phật" 108 times with virtual prayer beads
Keep rhythm on the wooden fish drum for 2 minutes
Sit quietly in the main hall for 5 minutes
Write a peaceful wish for everyone

moTa: Commemorates Shakyamuni Buddha's awakening beneath the bodhi tree after days of meditation. The story of Sujata's bowl of milk rice before that night recalls the Middle Way, neither too harsh nor too indulgent. A day to nurture mindfulness.
trangTri: A great bodhi tree in the middle of the courtyard
A statue of the Buddha meditating under the bodhi tree
A bowl of milk rice on a lotus leaf
The morning star in the early sky
nhiemVu: Meditate under the virtual bodhi tree for 5 minutes
Wake early to see the morning star or the sunrise
Eat one meal slowly, attentive to every bite
Water the bodhi tree and write one thing you have just understood

moTa: In Vietnamese folk belief, the 23rd day of the twelfth lunar month is when the Kitchen Gods return to heaven to report on the family's year. Many households clean the kitchen, prepare an offering tray and release carp. A time to tidy the home, look back on the year and prepare for Tết.
trangTri: Paper hats and robes of the Kitchen Gods
A basin of red carp
A freshly cleaned kitchen
Peach branches just beginning to bud
nhiemVu: Release a virtual carp into the lotus pond
Tidy your real kitchen or desk
Write a three-line review of your year
Sweep the temple courtyard to welcome the new year

ten: Year's End – New Year's Eve (Trừ Tịch)
moTa: The last day of the lunar year, with the year-end family meal and Trừ Tịch night, the moment of farewell to the old year and welcome to the new. Many people go to temples to hear the New Year's Eve bell. If the twelfth lunar month has only 29 days that year, the event takes place on the 29th.
trangTri: A year-end family meal tray
Virtual fireworks in the night sky
The great bell in the bell tower
Red lanterns across the courtyard
Green square sticky rice cakes (bánh chưng)
nhiemVu: Ring the virtual New Year's Eve bell
Write a thank-you to the passing year
Light incense to welcome the New Year
Send a New Year wish to someone you love
Sit in stillness at the moment the year turns
